articles.text: COVID cases now increasing statewide At a Piedmont City Council meeting on August 16 Mayor Teddy Gray King announced her intention to mandate vaccinations for all city employees. “This is a very dynamic issue,” she said. “We know that there are many members of the community who are already vaccinated. I’m requesting that our city attorney draft a proposal that would mandate that all members of our city staff receive a COVID vaccination as soon as it is cleared by the FDA.” One week later, on August 23, the Food and Drug Administration granted full approval to Pfizer’s coronavirus vaccine for individuals age 16 and older, paving the way for a mandate in Piedmont. King cited the emergence of the Delta variant as her rationale for the mandate, adding that many cities and school districts, including the Piedmont School District, have already set forth such mandates for employees. The city was also waiting for full FDA-approval for COVID- 19 vaccine to mandate vaccinations. King said that, although most city staff are already fully vaccinated, that she would like to see this enacted quickly. City Attorney Michelle Kenyon will draft a rule detailing the city’s expectations for staff. “It’s a step in the right direction,” King said, adding that a mandate would have come sooner but that pending FDA-approval limited the city’s ability to do so. Currently, 93% of fulltime and regular part-time city employees are vaccinated against COVID-19. Latest COVID numbers from State The California Department of Public Health on August 23 confirmed that COVID-19 cases are increasing statewide, largely among unvaccinated populations. For the week of August 9 through August 15, the average case rate among unvaccinated Californians was 51 per 100,000 per day. The average case rate among vaccinated Californians is much lower, at 7.6 per 100,000 per day. As of August 23, according to the Center for Disease Control (CDC), 79.4% of eligible Californians have received at least one dose of a COVID vaccine. Vaccinations are available for free. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department is gearing up for its 3rd annual Car Show on Labor Day morning, Monday, September 6. The lineup of cars will be on view in the parking lot in front of the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. The last time the event was held in 2019, 44 gleaming vehicles were on display. From classic cars to late model Ferraris and Bugattis, all the hottest vehicles and their proud owners will be there. After taking a hiatus in 2020 due to COVID- 19, the show has returned and the competition for first, second, and third place will be fierce. As part of the Police department’s outreach activities, coffee will be available as neighbors come to meet members of the police department while chatting with the car owners. The event is part of the larger “Coffee with a Cop” national campaign, which was started in 2016 as a way for residents to meet local law enforcement members. Pete’s Coffee will be donating the refreshments for the morning’s festivities. In 2018 more than 1600 people showed up for the Car Show that was spearheaded by retiring Sergeant Steve DeWarns. “I value the Piedmont Police Department Car Show because I believe it builds strong relationships between community members and their police department,” said Officer Tyler Petit who is coordinating the show. “The mutual trust between our police department and the community we serve is essential in maintaining public safety and effective policing. I’ll do whatever it takes to maintain that public trust.” Piedmont car owners interested in displaying their cars in the city’s version of a Concours d’Elegance are asked to contact Officer Petit at tpetit@ piedmont.ca.gov. Include your name, address, email, and phone number along with the year, make and model of your car. 1949 MG TC owned by Jack Stehr.
articles.title: PPD invites residents to display classic, exotic cars on Sept. 6

articles.text: “Hope is being able to see that there is light despite all of the darkness.” – Bishop Desmond Tutu The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public forum on the subject of carbon pricing on Wednesday, September 22 at 4:00 p.m. It will be on Zoom and also on the LWV YouTube channel. It is free for those registering at: lwvpiedmont.org/events. It’s a summer like no other here in California. Smoke and destruction from wildfires have already claimed more than 1 million acres in California alone; warmer oceans harbor zombie urchins destroying kelp forests; and the U.N. just released a new Code Red on climate change. Wondering where to look for hope despite the current darkness? Could something as arcane as carbon pricing offer a ray of light? It’s a hot topic as Congress seeks to up the ante on climate action. To learn more, join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, Citizens’ Climate Education and Piedmont Connect for a panel discussion on carbon pricing, followed by questions and answers. The event is free. Registration is required on the League’s website: lwvpiedmont.org/events. An economy-wide price on carbon promises to reduce carbon emissions quickly and at scale in a way that is equitable when combined with a carbon dividend that most benefits low-income Americans. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen testified earlier this year that “we cannot solve the climate crisis without effective carbon pricing.” The U.S. is one of only a few major industrialized nations without a national carbon pricing policy. Carbon pricing and dividends have gained the support of a wide array of groups including: an unlikely bipartisan coalition that unites Goldman Sachs with the World Wildlife Fund, 28 Nobel laureate economists, the Washington Post editorial board; our own Barbara Lee and 80 fellow House members; all five members of Piedmont’s City Council; and thousands of businesses, labor unions, faith groups and other prominent individuals around the country and around the Bay. Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King will offer introductory Mike Mielke, Senior Vice President and Head of Public Policy for the Silicon Valley Leadership Group (SLVG) remarks. A panel discussion will feature Mike Mielke, Senior Vice President and Head of Public Policy for the Silicon Valley Leadership Group (SLVG). Mike supports hundreds of innovation-economy companies to engage the public and wield influence in addressing pressing environmental challenges facing communities. He has held posts with the White House Council on Environmental Quality and the National Estuary Program.
articles.title: LWV to host forum on carbon pricing

articles.text: California to require patrons to show proof of vaccination or negative COVID-19 test California will require individuals attending indoor events with 1,000 or more people to show proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. The order goes into effect on September 20, according to an announcement on August 18 by the California Department of Public Health. The requirement strengthens already-existing requirements for “mega-events” of 5,000 attendees or more, as stated in Gov. Gavin Newsom’s “Beyond the Blueprint” Framework. The requirement essentially narrows the capacity for testing or proof of vaccination from 5,000 individuals to 1,000. Self-attestation to verify a person’s vaccination status, an honor system, will no longer be accepted. The changes are to remain in place until November 1. “The Delta variant has proven to be highly transmissible, making it easier to spread in large crowds where people are near each other for long periods of time,” said Dr. Tomás J. Aragón, CDPH Director and State Public Health Officer. “By requiring individuals to be vaccinated, or test negative for COVID-19 at large events, we are decreasing the risk of infection, hospitalization and death.” California has implemented strict measures across various industries to thwart the transmission of COVID-19 and its variants, as compared to other states in the nation. For example, the state has already required all school staff to show proof of full vaccination, or be tested once a week. The same applies for state workers. Full vaccination status is required for individuals who work in health care settings, as of September 30. In addition, California is the first state to implement universal mask-wearing in schools in all grade levels. The state recommended, but did not mandate, mask-wearing outdoors regardless of vaccination status. Leaders and professionals in the live entertainment industry praised the state for the recent announcement of health protocols for large gatherings. Julie Baker, Executive Director of Californians for the Arts, said, “We are pleased to see the Newsom administration take proactive steps to support the arts and live events industries to keep audiences, performers and workers safe as we continue to battle the spread of COVID.” “The arts have always led with safety first, and it is imperative that for every community’s economic, social and emotional recovery, we must do everything we can to allow for secure gatherings,” Baker said. “We implore Californians to get vaccinated and follow public health mandates so we can all enjoy the benefits of arts, culture and creativity, and our sector can get back to work.” COVID-19 vaccines are available to all California residents age 12 and older. For details, see: myturn.ca.gov, or call (833) 422- 4255 to schedule an appointment. The website myturn.ca.gov/clinic lists walk-in clinics in Alameda County. San Carlos Avenue. los Avenue.
articles.title: State to require all guests at indoor events to be vaccinated

CF Contracting of San Francisco was the lowest of six bids in the amount of $466,000. Work is estimated to begin in September, with a projected completion date of November. “[Residents adjacent to the project] are anxious to get this done,” said City Engineer John Wanger. Mayor Teddy Gray King added that former mayor Michael Bruck, who lives across from the retaining wall, brought the issue to her nearly seven years ago. “It’s been on our list for quite a while,” she said. articles.text: The arrangements were all set for Piedmont Troop 15 Scouts Ryan Tripp and Stewart James to receive their Eagle Scout awards in 2020, but the pandemic and shelter in place scratched their plans. A year and a half later, on Sunday, August 22, Ryan and Stew finally had their moment in the sun in a National Court of Honor ceremony on the patio of the Piedmont Community Center. Women took center stage in Ryan Tripp thanks fellow Eagle Stewart James (seated) during a Court of Honor at the Piedmont Community Center on August 22. Troop 15 Scoutmaster Glen Tripp describes the journey to the Eagle Award of Stewart James and Ryan Tripp. the celebration, illustrating the organization’s mission of character development for all youth in the community. Mayor Teddy Gray King led off the proceedings with City of Piedmont proclamations recognizing the Scouts’ achievements. Council Executive Kate Benson put the awards in context of Piedmont’s strong association with the Scouting movement. Troop 15 Chair Dana Mitchell recounted the significance of the Eagle badge, and new Troop 15 scout Christiane Zuber lit a candle in memory of Linda Trowbridge (1955-2021), who mentored several generations of Boy Scout Eagles and Girl Scout Gold Award recipients. Ryan Tripp Ryan Tripp is the son of Lauren Dutton and Glen Tripp, the Troop 15 Scoutmaster. His Eagle project was to expand access to crew through an innovative partnership between Oakland Strokes and West Oakland high schools, spreading the benefits of rowing to new populations. In his speech, Ryan mentioned how relevant his Scouting skills proved during his gap year camping in the Rocky Mountain wilderness and living on his own in Washington, D.C. Ryan is a graduate of Piedmont High School will attend Dartmouth College in the fall. Stewart James Stewart James is the son of Rob and Sarah James. Stew’s Eagle project was building a “chill zone” reading loft with learning materials for a thirdgrade classroom at Sequoia Elementary School in Oakland. His speech recounted his spiritual experience overcoming adversity and experiencing nature in a challenging hiking trek on Catalina Island. A graduate of the Drew School in San Francisco, Stew is a rising sophomore at Tufts University. Both Scouts are second generation Eagles. Rob James, the former President of the Piedmont Scout Council, received his Eagle Four Eagles: Stew James (2019), Rob James (1975), Ryan Tripp (2020), and Glen Tripp (1986). in 1975 in Salinas, and Glen Tripp received his Eagle in 1986 in Poway in Southern California. New Troop 15 senior patrol leader Schuyler Sawicki served as master of ceremonies for the event, attended by friends and family. There is no small irony to the fact that the Eagle has proven to be the most respected and bestknown award for American youth. What began as a badge of honor for a small coterie of dedicated teenagers has become not only the most enduring award for youth in American life, but also the most consistently rewarding award in their own lives. articles.text: On June 23 Piedmont School Board meetings returned in person for the first time since the Covid pandemic arrived a year and a half earlier. The meeting took place in the school district office boardroom at 760 Magnolia Avenue. Meetings will continue to be covered by KCOM on Channel 27 and on Zoom. The hybrid format allows all board members to meet in the same room with safety protocols, including masks. Members of the public now have the opportunity to contribute in person. “We will let members of the public in to speak in the public comment portion, so this is pretty exciting,” said Board President Cory Smegal. Visitors to any school site, including board meetings, must complete a visitor health screener online before entering the building. Board Member Hilary Cooper gave credit to Smegal for spearheading the initiative to return to traditional in-person meetings. “It was all Cory,” she said. “She felt very strongly that we should come together as a board in-person because we are asking our students and teachers to do the same.” The first in-person meeting lasted an hour and 45 minutes, a quick sprint in comparison to some marathon three- or fourhour zoom meetings last year. At the end of the June meeting, Smegal asked the room, “Do you think the meeting was shorter because we were in-person?” Board members universally nodded yes and Smegal replied, “Alright, this is the start of something great. This bodes well.” Since then, the board held another live meeting on August 11, which also finished in less than two hours. The board meets tonight, August 25 at 7:00 p.m. Meetings will continue to be held in the district office until given clearance by the City to return to Council Chambers in City Hall.
articles.title: School Board meetings return in person

articles.text: Nine Scouts in Piedmont’s Troop 4 recently attained the rank of Eagle at a Court of Honor ceremony. Pictured are Kevin Blodgett (left), Jonathan Wu, Kian Roseborough, Nate Wilson, Justin Katter, Gavin Horne, Linus Lee, Andrew Grasman, and Jack Blodgett. On Wednesday, August 18 Piedmont’s Troop 4 hosted an historic National Eagle Court of Honor with a record nine new Eagle Scouts being honored. Friends and families of Troop 4 gathered under the redwoods behind the Piedmont Community Center to help celebrate this hard-earned award. Special guest speakers included Mayor Teddy King, Scout Executive Kate Benson, and Rev. Scott Kail of Piedmont Community Church. Robert Barry Hamilton, the grandfather of Scout Andrew Grasman, an Eagle Scout, West Point graduate and military veteran, gave a keynote speech on the significance of the Eagle award. He advised the Scouts that they will face new challenges in their lives, and the right decision is not always easy to make. He also said, “When life gives you lemons, make lemonade.” For their Eagle projects, Jack Blodgett built a compost bin for Greenleaf Elementary School; Kevin Blodgett built a fruit box storage area for Piedmont Middle School; Andrew Grasman created a series of computer science videos for the James Baldwin Academy; Gavin Horne built an outdoor stage at the playground by the Piedmont Recreation Department; Justin Katter built a wooden cabinet for music binders for the PHS Acapella program; Linus Lee built a fence for dogs at the Hopalong Animal Shelter; Kian Roseborough built steps and reinforced a slope on a trail for the Friends of Sausal Creek; Nate Wilson installed exercise equipment storage units for Bay Area Outreach Program (BORP), which helps physically handicapped people be active; and Jonathan Wu installed a flagstone patio in back of Wildwood Elementary School. All of the Eagle Scouts thanked the Troop 4 leaders, parent volunteers, fellow Scouts, and their family and friends for their unwavering support to help them on their long journey to Eagle.

articles.text: Turn a gathering around the campfire into a perfect summer science lesson with this activity. Put a twist on the classic snack by packing marshmallows, chocolate and more into waffle cones for the ultimate summer treat. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions. When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that began as solid ingredients (chocolate and marshmallows) begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team opens its fall season this Friday, August 27, with a game against non-league opponent Miramonte in Orinda. With the sports world returning to normal, Piedmont will have an 11-game game schedule. But with the graduation of half of the varsity roster, this will be a rebuilding season. Coach Jerome Johnson has only 16-17 players on the varsity. In a shortened season, Piedmont had a perfect 5-0 record last spring. “This particular class does not have large numbers,” confirmed Johnson. “Right after the COVID-year, more kids haven’t returned due to whatever factors there may be. The class before this loved football. We knew our numbers would be low, but not this low. We were hoping that the success we had after going 5-0 would have built more excitement for football,” he said. Last year’s football program didn’t have a JV team, making a noticeable impact on this year’s team. In the spring of 2021 student-athletes were forced to choose between baseball and football, which had the same season. A few of those players are back, like Nico Defazio and Evan McConathy. articles.text: Almost every parent I know feels bad about their parenting. If you’re anything like them, these are some of the things you feel bad about: You feel bad because you don’t spend enough time with your kids. You feel bad because you spend too much time with your kids. You feel bad because your kids spend too much time online. You feel bad because you secretly like it when your kids spend too much time online because it gives you a break. You feel bad because you don’t spend enough time helping your kids with their homework. You feel bad because you spend too much time helping your kids with their homework (and their grades aren’t even improving, which makes you feel even worse). And mostly, you feel bad because if you didn’t feel bad, and if you actually felt confident and at ease about your parenting, this would mean you’re doing something really, really wrong. Sound familiar? Feeling bad about your parenting isn’t your fault. Parents today are bombarded with messages about how to parent, and the Parenting Industrial Complex, as I call it, would collapse if parents relied on their instincts, common sense, and the support of friends and family to parent. So, in this age of Feel Bad Parenting, I’d like to offer some relief. First of all, you’re doing a great job as a parent. Seriously, Giving yourself a high five as a parent will make you feel better instantly. everything is fine. And I’m going to prove it to you. For the next week, spend 5-10 minutes every day creating a list of all the things you do well as a parent. Write down everything you can think of--no achievement is too small. The only caveat is that if/when a negative thought about your parenting pops into your head you must dismiss it immediately. Your list of positive parenting achievements might include: 1. I work hard (in or outside of the home) to provide for my kids 2. I love my kids more than anything in the world (most of the time) 3. I would do anything for my kids Every parent I know can say these things. And this is fantastic. You need to know that parenting will get easier, and you (and your kids) will feel happier when you stop feeling bad about yourself as a parent. If you create a list of all the things you do well as a parent, and keep it up daily for just one week, you will start to feel better. I promise. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.

articles.text: MS, OTR/L Are you beginning to think that handwriting is obsolete? This is certainly a valid thought given our students’ dependency on keyboarding assignments instead of handwriting them over the last year due to the pandemic. Keyboarding is always legible and who doesn’t like spell check? At a recent IEP (Individualized Education Plan) meeting for a student that I serve, the topic of handwriting versus keyboarding was raised. Lists can be made on phones, letters sent by email and essays written using Google documents. In short, is handwriting even necessary? To this question, the answer is a resounding Yes. Recent research, comparing handwriting to keyboarding, found handwriting improves memory/recall, comprehension, and even test scores. Handwriting remains an essential skill for both younger and older students, including those in college. Three recent studies noted the following: • Preschool students were taught to copy letters of the alphabet by hand or by typing them. After three weeks of learning, letter recognition tests were completed. The older preschool students in the handwriting instruction/ practice group demonstrated better letter recognition – a fundamental skill for learning letter sounds and reading (Longcamp et al, 2005). One study compared methods of note taking, handwritten or typed, and the recall and understanding of children 10–11 years old. articles.text: Twilight Camp, an early camping experience for six- and sevenyear-olds, is a Piedmont tradition going back two generations and sponsored by the Piedmont Scout Council. It will be held this year from Tuesday to Thursday. October 26-28, from 7:00 to 8:30 p.m. each night. Register at https:// www.piedmontbsa.org/events/ twilight-camp/. Early Bird signups at $35 are available until October 15. The cost after that is $40. The registration deadline is October 22. Twilight Camp is open to all boys and girls in 1st and 2nd grades. They can look forward to building and racing rain gutter regatta boats, and making fun snacks. It’s a great opportunity to escape the indoors and have some outdoor fun, and to experience Scouting at its best. The opening ceremony each evening is in the amphitheater behind the Piedmont Community Center after which campers will rotate through stations. In one of the favorite activities, the rain gutter regatta, campers build a boat on the first night. On night two, they paint it, and on the third night they get to use their own wind power to propel it along the rain gutter. “It is great to look forward to this event again,” said new Scout Executive Kate Benson. “The evenings in October are cool and just dark enough to be spooky fun.” While activities are geared towards younger Cub Scouts, all grade school students are welcome to register and enjoy the fun. Fun is important, but safety is the highest priority. “Keeping campers safe, whether from COVID or other concerns, is part of every step of planning,” said Benson. “Every step of safety, at home and at camp, is vital.” Safety steps include pre-camp health screenings done by parents, frequent handwashing, and hand sanitizing, and moving from station to station in cohorts. Even though all activities will be done outdoors, campers and parents will mask up as well. Attendance will be taken each day, and the lines of communication will be wide open with parents. Campers and parents may need to present a negative COVID test or vaccination in advance of camp. “County guidelines could be fluid as we approach camp,” said Benson, “but we will work hard to keep campers, staff and parents safe. It is vital for our kids to have these types of activities. We saw just how important this past year and a half, and we’re excited to see everyone.” For more information and to register, navigate to www.piedmontbsa.org. Cub Scouting serves girls and boys in kindergarten through 5th grade and is fun for the whole family. It’s fun, hands-on learning with achievements that put kids in the middle of the action and prepares them for life. Cub Scouts at Twilight Camp enjoy racing their boats in the Raingutter Regatta.

articles.text: The Benjamin Jazz Trio will perform at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, August 29 at 5 p.m. He will be joined by Bay Area musicians Dahveed Behroozi on piano and Zachary Ostroff on bass. An accomplished composer, his first composition was premiered by the San Francisco Conservatory of Music percussion ensemble when he was 15. He has been recognized by festivals and institutions worldwide for his work in jazz and classical idioms. He graduated from USC with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2019, and will enter the Herbie Hancock Institute of Jazz Performance at UCLA this fall, a prestigious, 2-year Master’s program comprised of a small ensemble chosen by audition from across the globe. Dahveed Behroozi Pianist and Composer Dahveed Behroozi is a San Francisco Bay Area based musician. His focus is in jazz, classical, and new music. articles.text: It was a 1976 young conductors’ competition of the Baltimore Symphony, with a predictable array of well-scrubbed young men in their early- to mid-20s competing. And in this group appeared a striking youth, barely 17, seemingly from another world, wearing the casual togs he wore for any day at his public high school. For the finals he conducted a movement from a Brahms symphony that lifted me to my feet to watch intently. He evoked ear-caressing sounds of ethereal beauty, sounds I had not heard any of the far more experienced competitors achieve. This was a youth with the makings of genius, doing it all with the confidence of a veteran. This was the unlikely beginning of Michael Morgan, symphony conductor. He won none of the three prizes awarded, given merely a “nice-try” honorable mention. The Music Professor Elliott Galkin on the judges’ panel dismissed him as having no real conducting technique nor discipline. Perhaps. But for this listener, he had made the sounds to lift both heart and soul. The untimely death of Morgan this week of an infection at age 63 closed out a mercurial career the last 30 years of which were as music director of the Oakland Symphony – the longest tenure in the orchestra’s history. Coming from modest circumstances in Washington, DC, he got recommendations and a scholarship aid to enter the elite Oberlin Conservatory of Music and was selected to study one summer under Leonard Bernstein’s tutelage at Tanglewood, MA. Still in his 20s he appeared at the Vienna State Opera to lead a Mozart performance and was appointed the assistant conductor of the Chicago Symphony under the venerable Georg Solti, no less. But his real forte evolved during his 30-year stint at the helm of the Oakland Symphony. He turned out to be an exemplary community builder, drawing unprecedented black listeners to the concerts and annotating his concerts with self-effacing wit. Recently leading the Charleston with the San Francisco Symphony, he quipped that yes, the Charleston had been the dance that epitomized the Roaring Twenties. “We’re hoping for another Roaring Twenties, but without the crash at the end….,” he said. He brought in performers of many forms of music, including Latino, jazz, African-American and Far-Eastern, and works by contemporary women composers. He also rescued from oblivion the exemplary Symphony No. 3 (1847) by the French woman Louise Farrenc, performing it recently on both sides of San Francisco Bay. articles.text: Oakland Symphony announced on August 20 the death of its Music Director Michael Morgan. Its press release stated, “It is with a breaking heart that we inform you that Michael Morgan, Music Director and Conductor of Oakland Symphony since 1991, died peacefully today, August 20, 2021 at Oakland Kaiser where he had been admitted last week for an infection. He was 63.” In May of this year, Michael Morgan underwent successful kidney transplant surgery at UCSF. He resumed conducting last month for the San Francisco Symphony and Bear Valley Music Festival. Michael was born in Washington, D.C., where he attended public schools and began conducting at the age of 12. While a student at Oberlin College Conservatory of Music, he spent a summer at the Berkshire Music Center at Tanglewood, studying with Gunther Schuller and Seiji Ozawa. He first worked with Leonard Bernstein during that same summer. His operatic debut was in 1982 at the Vienna State Opera, conducting Mozart’s The Abduction from the Seraglio. In 1986, Sir Georg Solti chose him to become the Assistant Conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, a position he held for seven years under both Solti and Daniel Barenboim. In 1986, he was invited by Leonard Bernstein to make his debut with the New York Philharmonic. As guest conductor, Morgan has appeared with most of America’s major orchestras, as well as the New York City Opera, St. Louis Opera Theater, and Washington National Opera. In addition to his duties with the Oakland Symphony, Maestro Morgan served as Artistic Director of Oakland Symphony Youth Orchestra, Music Director at Bear Valley Music Festival, and Music Director of Gateways Music Festival. He was Music Director Emeritus of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera and was on the boards of Oaktown Jazz Workshops and the Purple Silk Music Education Foundation. He was also a former music director of Festival Opera in Walnut Creek, and “Notes From…” concer ts explored the music and musicians of such specific communities as Vietnam, Korea, Native American and LGBTQ+. “Lost Romantics” gave deserving, neglected works of the late 19th century a new hearing. “American Masterworks” presented performances of such seminal stage works as West Side Story, Candide, Street Scene, Porgy and Bess, and Show Boat. The San Francisco Chronicle proclaimed, “In his 30 years as music director of the Oakland Symphony, Morgan has made that orchestra a vibrant hotbed for innovative programming.” “Our entire organization is grieving a profound loss,” said Jim Hasler, Oakland Symphony Board Chair. “Michael’s impact on our community and the national orchestra field cannot be overstated – and he has left us too soon. We have been blessed over the past 30 years, as Michael built the foundations of an Oakland Symphony dedicated to diversity, education, artistic collaboration, and a celebration of music across genres and cultures. His vision of orchestras as service organizations was a beacon locally and nationally. This vision is his legacy, and the Oakland Symphony, Chorus and Youth Orchestra will renew his commitment for years to come.” “This is a terribly sad moment for everyone in the Oakland Symphony family. We have lost our guiding father,” said Executive Director Mieko Hatano. “Michael’s plans and ambitions were set for several seasons to come. He made his Orchestra socially authentic, demanded equality, and he made his Orchestra our orchestra. He fashioned a unique, informed artistic profile that attracted one of the most diverse audiences in the nation. His music reflected his beliefs: reverence for the past, attuned to the future, rooted in his adopted home of Oakland. His spirit will always guide the enduring future of the Oakland Symphony.” Michael Morgan is survived by his mother Mabel Morgan, and sister Jacquelyn Morgan. A memorial service will be announced in the near future. Oakland Symphony Music Director Michael Morgan died on August 20, 2021. articles.text: Most of us don’t think about global warming when we buy that cute, bargain hoody or jazzy top. And yet, “fast fashion” — mass produced, inexpensive, trendy clothing — has become one of the world’s biggest consumers of natural resources and contributor to climate change. The amount of clothing sold every year has approximately doubled in the last 15 years and now exceeds 100 billion garments per year. From production to disposal, the impact of clothing on the environment is astounding. Consider that it takes nearly 4,000 gallons of water to grow cotton for one pair of jeans and 2,700 gallons for a t-shirt. At least 8,000 chemicals are used to turn raw materials into textiles, and 25 percent of the world’s pesticides are used to grow non-organic cotton. The popular use of polyester and other synthetic fibers by the textile industry now accounts for nearly 1.5% of total global oil consumption and is expected to double in coming years. The Fossil Fashion campaign, which advocates legislation to curtail the fashion industry’s use of fossil fuels, calculates washing clothes releases around half a million tons of microfibers into the oceans every year, equal to more than 50 billion plastic bottles. And what happens to all the clothes Americans throw away every year? Second-hand stores sell only about 10% of our donated clothes. The remaining 90% is sold to textile recyclers who process about 70% into rags and cleaning cloths. Some used clothing is sold on the international market, but eventually twothirds of discarded clothing material ends up in massive landfills, primarily in African and other third-world countries. The fact that our clothing consumption is environmentally devastating has become a wake-up call in the fashion industry. A number of industry leaders have embraced the concept of a “circular economy” in which nothing is wasted in the manufacturing process. Some, including H&M, Ralph Lauren, LaCoste, and Tommy Hilfiger, have begun making clothes from recycled or eco-friendly fabrics, and using renewable energy. There is also a “slow fashion” trend gaining traction. Echoing the Slow Food movement, slow fashion emphasizes buying fewer but better quality, more durable clothes that last longer, are less fashion-trendy and that value fair treatment of the planet, animals and workers in their life cycle. According to the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, doubling the use of our clothes would cut the garment trade’s climate pollution by nearly half. In addition, more of us have discovered the fun of shopping at second hand stores, such as Dress Best For Less (DBFL) on Piedmont Ave., which supports the Piedmont Education Foundation and other local nonprofits. For a more complete list of local second-hand stores, visit https:// www.piedmontconnect.org Even Macy’s has launched a thredUp shop that carries second-hand styles from top brands. And TheRealReal, an online, luxury consignment store. buys and sells clothes and other goods has an outlet in San Francisco. Perhaps the words of legendary folksinger Pete Seeger will become the new fashion mantra: “If it can’t be reduced, repaired, rebuilt, refurbished, refinished, resold, recycled or composted, then it should be restricted, redesigned or removed from production.”

Dear Jim: We are about to embark on a large home improvement project but have been hearing horror stories about the cost of materials, contractors backed up for months or years to start projects and that it’s almost impossible to get permits, etc. How should we navigate all of this? Would it be better to wait to see if conditions improve? -Edward M. Residential construction is currently experiencing substantial challenges. Let’s look briefly into these issues and sort out fact from fiction. Permits Permitting has been a nightmare for the last 18 months in most jurisdictions. Though residential contractors were generally allowed to keep working during Covid, all building departments went online with not-so-great results. Permits, on average, are taking several months for simple projects and much longer for complicated ones. Many factors are involved, such as layoffs, employees with Covid, and people retiring. It has been mostly a major communication debacle caused when people are not working in person. We have seen this improve recently, as building departments are now opening to the public and backlogs are being reduced. Materials and Labor Costs Lumber prices were highly impacted by Covid. Sawmills shut down just as a housing boom surged, causing massive price increases, as much as 500% or more for items like plywood. Materials from overseas (such as steel, cabinets, tile) saw large shipping cost increases and huge delays. I waited for 6 months for a tile ordered from Spain which sat for three months in the harbor in New York under quarantine. Demand for labor is at an all-time high, with construction workers demanding higher wages and benefits. Contractor Availability and Pricing. With more people choosing to work from home when they can, home improvement project requests have skyrocketed. Prices that contractors are charging for their work are reflected in higher estimates. Since most of us are busy and permitting is delayed, projects are getting pushed farther out into the future. Additionally, estimates that were given even 6 months ago may have to be adjusted to reflect new increases in costs. The Bottom Line Construction keeps getting more expensive. It’s hard to find a good contractor, and projects are having substantial delays. Though some of this may improve slightly if permitting timeframes decrease, there is no indication that costs or contractors’ workloads will lessen anytime soon. Your best bet would be to try to get your project onto your contractor’s calendar as overall conditions will likely remain challenging into the foreseeable future. Five hours of rain on the first night refreshed the wildflowers, and didn’t seem to dampen the Scouts’ spirits. “The trek was challenging at times, but overall it was a great experience,” said Scout Trenton Downing. On day hikes the scouts spotted marmots, water snakes, bullfrogs, and ducks. Scouts practiced parkour bouldering on glacier-carved granite benches that stair-stepped the way to ridge summits. The rewards were expansive vistas of the volcanic spires of Castle Rock and Three Chimneys to the north, and The Granite Dome to the east. The Scouts cooked their breakfast and had their packs on ready to go by 8 a.m. each day. “My favorite meal was breakfast – oatmeal with raisins, mango, nuts and brown sugar,” said seventh grader Morgan Bishop. The geology shows signs of major fractures in the mountains. Chewing Gum Lake at sunset. Scouts cool off in Chewing Gum Lake after hours of hiking. For dinners, Scouts enjoyed chicken tikka masala, pita stuffed with spinach and cucumbers, falafel with tahini-lemon sauce, and couscous chicken with green beans and asparagus – tasty eating in the High Sierra. The Scouts practiced LeaveNo-Trace and the Outdoor Code by packing out everything they brought on the hike. All the Scouts worked on their Camping, Backpacking and Hiking merit badges. “We really got to experience the outdoors. We filtered our drinking water and we got to swim in the refreshing lake water,” said Sammy Ragones. More fun with Troop 15 Troop 15 Scouts will be spending this coming weekend, August 28-29, at Point Reyes National Seashore, with a 10-mile hike, cooking meals, and receiving training in the use of knives, saws, and axes. Interested in the outdoors and personal development? Girls and boys ages 11 to 17 and their parents are invited to contact Scoutmaster Glen Tripp at Glen@Galileo-learning.com for details.
